How Much Does Landscaping Cost in The Hills Shire?

How much does landscaping cost in The Hills Shire? A 2026 guide to realistic price ranges for design, paving, turf and retaining walls. Free quotes.

HS Hills Shire Landscaping 7 min read Free on-site quotes · The Hills Shire

props.label: What actually drives the cost
props.html:
Planning a garden project in The Hills Shire and trying to work out a budget? Landscaping costs can look all over the place, and that’s because no two blocks or briefs are the same. This 2026 guide gives you honest price ranges for the area, explains what actually drives the cost, and shows where the money tends to go. Hillshire Landscaping designs and builds gardens right across The Hills Shire, from Castle Hill to Kellyville and Baulkham Hills, so while only a site visit gives a real figure, this will get you close enough to plan.

Quick answer

Landscaping in The Hills Shire typically ranges from a few thousand dollars for smaller garden refreshes to tens of thousands for a full design-and-construction backyard makeover. Final cost depends on site size, slope, materials, and how much hard landscaping like paving and retaining walls is involved. Always get an on-site quote for landscape design and construction.

What actually drives the cost

A handful of things decide where your project lands, and understanding them explains why two quotes for similar-looking gardens can differ by thousands.

  • Size of the areaThe bigger the space, the more materials, planting and labour, so square metreage is the natural starting point.
  • Slope and accessA flat, open block is straightforward, while a sloping site or one with narrow side access needs terracing, retaining and materials carried in by hand, which adds cost fast. Plenty of Hills blocks around Dural, Glenhaven and Kellyville sit on a grade.
  • How much hard landscaping is involvedPaving, retaining walls, decking and structures are the big-ticket items, and they take the largest share of most budgets.
  • MaterialsBudget concrete or treated pine sits at one end, natural stone, premium pavers and hardwood at the other, and the choice can double a single line item.
  • Drainage and site prepThe unglamorous groundwork that makes everything last, and it’s money well spent even though you can’t see it once it’s done.
  • Design complexityA simple tidy-up is one thing; a full design with levels, zones and features is another.

Most of these come back to one theme: the more built structure and premium material in the plan, the higher the total. It’s why a landscaper will always want to see the block before putting a number on it. A useful way to think about it is that labour and access set the baseline, materials set the finish, and how much structure you build sets the ceiling on the total.

Typical price ranges by project type

Here are broad Hills Shire guide ranges for 2026. Treat them as a starting point only, since your block and brief decide the real figure, and an on-site quote is the only accurate price.

Project typeGuide range (2026)
Small garden refresh (turf, mulch, planting, tidy-up)~$3,000 to $10,000
Mid-size backyard makeover (paving, new turf, planting, edging)~$15,000 to $40,000
Full design and construction (retaining, paving, decking, drainage, premium finishes)~$50,000 to $100,000+
Landscape design / concept planfrom ~$3,000

Most established Hills homes land in the mid-range once you combine some paving, planting and a structure or two. A separate design or concept plan is common on the bigger jobs, and it’s money well spent, because a considered plan stops expensive changes mid-build and keeps the whole project heading the same way. It’s also worth remembering these are whole-project figures, so a quote that looks cheap may only cover part of the scope. Always check what’s actually included before comparing one quote against another.

Why sloped blocks cost more

A lot of The Hills Shire is anything but flat, and slope is one of the biggest cost multipliers in landscaping. A sloping block usually needs retaining walls to create level, usable space, extra excavation and drainage to manage runoff, and more labour to work safely on the grade. Where a flat yard might just need turf and planting, a sloping one needs the structure built first, and that groundwork is where the budget goes. Good retaining walls are often the foundation of a sloping-block garden, both literally and in the quote.

Soft vs hard landscaping

It helps to split a project into two buckets, because they cost very differently. Hard landscaping is the built structure: paving, retaining walls, decking, paths, edging and drainage. It’s material- and labour-heavy, and it’s where most of the budget goes on a bigger job. Soft landscaping is the living side: turf, plants, trees, mulch and garden beds. It’s generally cheaper per square metre and is what brings the space to life once the structure is in.

A smart budget usually prioritises the hard landscaping first, since retaining, drainage and paving are hard and expensive to retrofit later, then adds planting and finishing touches, which can even be staged over time as budget allows. New turf laying and planting are the classic final step that make a finished garden look the part. Getting the balance right, and the order right, is a big part of what a good landscaper brings to the table, and it’s often where a design pays for itself. On a typical Hills backyard, the hard landscaping and site works often account for well over half the total, with planting and turf making up the rest, which is worth keeping in mind when you set your budget.

How to get an accurate quote

The honest truth is that any figure in a guide like this is a ballpark, and the only real number comes from someone standing in your yard. On site, a landscaper can see the slope, the access, the soil and drainage, and what’s already there, then price the specific materials and structures your plan needs. That’s why a written, itemised quote after an inspection is worth far more than a rough number over the phone. It also lets you compare quotes properly, since you can see who’s included the groundwork, drainage and prep and who’s quietly left them out to look cheaper. A quote that spells out each element is itself a sign of a landscaper who works properly. When you’re ready for a real figure, it starts with a free on-site quote. It’s worth getting two or three quotes and comparing them line by line, since the cheapest headline number is rarely the cheapest job once the missing items are added back in.

Frequently asked questions

Is a landscaping quote free?

Reputable Hills Shire landscapers generally provide a free, no-obligation quote after an on-site visit, since seeing the block is the only way to price it accurately. A separate paid fee usually only applies to a detailed design or concept plan, which is a different service. Always confirm what’s included when you book.

What’s the most cost-effective landscaping improvement?

For value on a budget, fresh turf, tidy garden beds, mulch and defined edging deliver the biggest visual lift for the least spend, and they’re quick to do. Kerb appeal from a neat, green front garden is where many homeowners get the best return. Bigger structural work costs more but adds usable living space.

Does a bigger budget always mean a better result?

Not necessarily. A well-designed, well-built garden on a modest budget often beats an expensive one built without a plan. Spending on the right things, structure, drainage and quality where it counts, matters more than spending big everywhere. A considered design makes a smaller budget go further, which is why planning first is worth it.

Final thoughts

Landscaping cost in The Hills Shire comes down to the size of the job, the slope of the block, the materials and how much built structure is involved. Use the ranges here to plan a budget, prioritise the groundwork, and get the design right before the build. For a figure tailored to your place, Hillshire Landscaping can help.
